Figure 1 – Cloud Actors
A conceptual diagram showing five cloud-computing actors arranged as labeled rounded rectangles over a blue cloud-shaped background. No arrows or connector lines are visible; the relationships are conveyed by the actor descriptions and spatial arrangement. The actors and their visible text are:

1) Cloud Consumer (upper left): "Person, or organization that maintains a business relationship with, and uses service from Cloud Providers".
2) Cloud Provider (center): "Person, organization or entity responsible for making a service available to Cloud Consumers".
3) Cloud Broker (upper right): "An entity that manages the use, performance and delivery of cloud services, and negotiates relationships between Cloud Providers and Cloud Consumers".
4) Cloud Auditor (lower left): "A party that can conduct independent assessment of cloud services, information system operations, performance and security of the cloud implementation".
5) Cloud Carrier (bottom, spanning width): "The intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services from Cloud Providers to Cloud Consumers".

Visual layout: Cloud Consumer and Cloud Auditor are stacked on the left; Cloud Provider is centered and tallest; Cloud Broker is on the right; Cloud Carrier is a long horizontal box beneath the three upper boxes. The background includes overlapping blue cloud shapes behind the boxes.

Arbitrage: Service arbitrage is similar to service aggregation except that the services being
           combined/consolidated  are not  fixed. Service  arbitrage means a Broker has  the
              flexibility to choose services from multiple service Providers.

A Cloud Broker may provide:

    1.   Business and relationship support services (business intermediation), and

    2.   Technical support service (aggregation, arbitrage, and technical intermediation), with a
        key focus on handling interoperability issues among multiple Providers.

4.6   CLOUD CARRIER

A cloud carrier acts as an intermediary that provides connectivity and transport of cloud services
between cloud consumers and cloud providers. Cloud carriers provide access to consumers through
network, telecommunication, and other access devices. For example, cloud consumers can obtain
cloud services through network access devices, such as computers, laptops, mobile phones, mobile
Internet devices (MIDs), etc. The distribution of cloud services is normally provided by network
and telecommunication carriers or a transport agent, where a transport agent refers to a business
organization that provides physical transport of storage media such as high-capacity hard drives.
Note that a cloud provider will set up service level agreements (SLAs)20 with a cloud carrier to
provide services consistent with the level of SLAs offered to cloud consumers, and may require the
cloud carrier to provide dedicated and encrypted connections between cloud consumers and cloud
providers.

Figure 12
The Combined Conceptual Reference Diagram for cloud computing. A large blue rounded rectangle encloses several role areas. On the left is a vertical block labeled Cloud Consumer at top and Cloud Auditor below; within Cloud Auditor are three stacked boxes: Security Audit, Privacy Impact Audit, and Performance Audit. In the center is Cloud Provider, containing two main sections: Cloud Orchestration and Cloud Service Management. Under Cloud Orchestration is a Service Layer with three overlapping service boxes labeled SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS, above a Resource Abstraction and Control Layer, and below that a Physical Resource Layer containing Hardware and Facility. In the Cloud Service Management section are three stacked boxes labeled Business Support, Provisioning/Configuration, and Portability/Interoperability. On the right is Cloud Broker with three stacked boxes: Service Intermediation, Service Aggregation, and Service Arbitrage. Along the bottom spanning the diagram is Cloud Carrier, with a caption beneath inside the frame reading Cross Cutting Concerns: Security, Privacy, etc. The figure is a conceptual block diagram showing relationships among roles and service layers rather than a plot; no arrows are visible.

No explicit arrows or connector lines are visible in the figure; relationships are inferred from grouping and placement.
